basis: New mission, no workbook source. Facts: Taiwan 2024 generation ~11.6% renewables with wind generation +66% 2023->2024 (variability now a material grid share); 3 March 2022 cascading blackout triggered by a single switch malfunction at Hsinta Power Plant, Kaohsiung, cutting power to ~5.49M households (~40% of Taiwan) via cascading grid protection trips (Taiwan News/Bloomberg/CommonWealth); TSMC ~9% of national electricity, semiconductor/data-centre demand rising and less predictable (SDxCentral/TrendForce); Taipower reached ~1GW (1,000MW) of grid-connected battery storage in 2025, incl. the Dongshan 60MW site (operating Nov 2024) and a 20MW system at the Tainan salt-field solar farm (Taipower press releases); Taipower AMI/smart-meter rollout passed 3.5M customers (>80% of consumption) by May 2025, target 6M by 2030 and full replacement by 2035, plus a DER Integration program under Taipower's Smart Grid effort; Taiwan storage market ~1GW/3GWh and >1% of global electrochemical storage by 2025, projected toward 20GWh by 2030, market value ~US$3.1bn (2025) toward ~US$9.8bn (2031) (Infolink-group, Mobility Foresights); LFP batteries ~90% of new grid-scale storage worldwide, trading energy density for thermal stability, longer cycle life (thousands of cycles, 10-15+ years) and lower cost versus NMC/NCA chemistries used in EVs; private-sector example of a Fluence-partnered 100-MW-class storage project. Register per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md. slides.1: Once the sun sets or the wind falls completely still, conventional generation alone cannot keep the lights on. This discussion investigates precisely where that missing power is actually supposed to come from.
slides.2: SDG 7 actually covers more than clean generation alone. It equally demands reliability, meaning power that keeps flowing whatever the weather, so today's focus falls squarely on modern, resilient infrastructure.
slides.3: Although rarely discussed outside engineering circles, Taiwan's power grid has already buckled once before under pressure. A single switch failure back in 2022 cascaded into serious outages across a wide share of the island.
slides.4: Renewable generation now dominates the grid's day-to-day swings in output. Wind generation alone has climbed roughly 66 percent in a single year, complicating forecasting far beyond what planners once assumed.
slides.5: Back in 2022, a fault in just one switch located in the south rippled outward, cascading across three separate regional grids at once. Within minutes, almost 5.5 million households were left without electricity.
slides.6: Chip plants now use an enormous and steadily growing share of national power. One firm alone accounts for roughly 9 percent of total demand that older infrastructure was never designed for.
slides.7: Battery storage on Taiwan's whole grid has now passed one full gigawatt in total. That milestone came partly from the Dongshan site, which first started running back in November 2024.
slides.8: More than 3.5 million customers across Taiwan now have a Taipower smart meter installed, covering upwards of 80 percent of the country's total power consumption. That constant flow of data is exactly what a modern grid depends on.
slides.9: Taiwan's whole energy-storage sector has expanded from a fairly tiny niche into an industry worth billions of dollars today. One projection expects continued rapid growth all the way through 2030.
slides.10: Rather than the energy-dense chemistry used in electric cars, most new grid-scale batteries rely on a chemistry known as LFP. That choice trades away some range for durability, safety and lower cost.
slides.11: Built for thousands of charge cycles, LFP cells also resist fire remarkably well. That combination suits stationary grid storage far better than the raw energy density that vehicles prize, while keeping overall costs relatively low.
slides.12: Taipower increasingly prefers software-driven routing over building yet another power plant, shifting electricity across the grid in near real time. Rooftop solar panels, home batteries and electric cars are steadily being absorbed into that very same network.
slides.13: A larger set of sensors and connected software creates more entry points for attackers to try. Only when a system's defences are fully secured will that added risk actually diminish over time.
slides.14: This whole fast-growing storage industry benefits Taiwan's broader technology sector quite considerably. Yet someone still has to bear the cost of every battery and meter, typically through higher electricity tariffs.
slides.15: Wealthier households nowadays tend to gain access to smart meters, home batteries and electric vehicles first. Poorer households may have to wait much longer, widening a gap that policy alone must address.
slides.16: The very same tools that resolve one technical problem can quietly generate several brand-new ones. A smart grid must therefore be judged on safety and fairness first, not efficiency alone.
slides.17: Piece by piece, and without ever fully switching off, Taiwan's electrical grid is undergoing a quiet transformation. Fresh batteries, sensors and control software now coexist with infrastructure that has, in some cases, served the island for decades.
slides.18: Few people outside this room will feel this dilemma as directly as the engineers, computer scientists and materials scientists seated here right now. It is you who will ultimately shape the next battery, algorithm or safety protocol.
slides.19: Learn to see the whole system rather than any single isolated component. Keep interrogating who actually gains access to these new tools first, and who is left waiting behind everyone else.
slides.20: A truly modern grid must be more than simply clean, since it also needs to be genuinely intelligent, resilient and equitable for everyone involved. The switch flipped in this very room belongs to a system you can now help design.
